items.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: all the young guys wanted to play “Sing Sing Sing” like Gene Krupa

ctx.x: You listen to the masters. You duplicate your masters until you find it yourself, until you get it. And then you can be yourself. But everybody comes from somewhere. The history, you know you listen to the guys that originated the stuff. Listen to Kenny Clarke, you listen to Art Blakey. You know what I’m saying? You listen to Papa Jo Jones. You listen to Philly Joe Jones. These are the guys that I like, that I listen to, to see just how they emphasize a phrase, you see what I’m saying? And to see how they just…

same phrase — you might love him to death man, but you don’t want to play the same thing he played in the same places. It gets stale. Because jazz is not like that. I mean this, in the beginning when you were a kid and all the young guys wanted to play “Sing Sing Sing” like Gene Krupa. You know that was a show that you really listened to Gene and you’d say, “man I can play ‘Sing Sing Sing.’” But man you’ve got to get away from that. You’ve got to be yourself. You’ve got to learn how to express how you feel see…

You mentioned earlier on in our talk about the Gospel influence. Tell us how that finds its way into the music. And I want to mention a term here, and then you take off on it. There’s a term that deals with several West African languages, called significant tone. And that means that the way that you pronounce a word, whether you give a higher inflection or a lower inflection to that tone, actually changes the meaning of the tone.
